A typical handler receives a JSON payload and returns a JSON result. A handler can also receive and
return streams. Use a stream for data that is too large for one JSON message, or for data that the
sender makes over time.

A stream that the handler receives is an `InputStream` to read or an `OutputStream` to write. A
stream that the handler returns is a value in its result. When the handler returns or throws, the
SDK closes, aborts, or cancels each stream that the handler received. See
[Manage the Stream lifecycle](#manage-the-stream-lifecycle).

<Note>
  To call functions with streams, read streams, and create pipes, see [Using iii /
  Streaming](../using-iii/streaming). For how a stream works, see [Understanding iii /
  Streaming](../understanding-iii/streaming). To move code from the channel API, see [Upgrading from
  0.26.x](../upgrading/from-0-26-x).
</Note>

## Receive a stream

When the caller sends a stream in a field of the payload, the handler receives an `InputStream` in
that field. The payload does not contain the data. The handler reads the data from the stream.

A stream has one reader, so read each `InputStream` one time only. For the read operations, see
[Read a stream from a result](../using-iii/streaming#read-a-stream-from-a-result).

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">

    ```typescript
    import { registerWorker, type InputStream } from "iii-sdk";

    const worker = registerWorker(process.env.III_URL ?? "ws://localhost:49134");

    worker.registerFunction(
      "files::process",
      async ({ filename, body }: { filename: string; body: InputStream }) => {
        let bytes = 0;
        for await (const chunk of body) bytes += chunk.length;
        return { filename, bytes };
      },
    );
    ```

    ```rust
    use schemars::JsonSchema;
    use serde::Deserialize;

    #[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
    struct Upload {
        filename: String,
        body: InputStream,

    worker.register_function(
        "files::process",
        RegisterFunction::new_async(|upload: Upload| async move {
    ```

    ```go
    type upload struct {
    	Filename string           `json:"filename"`
    	Body     *iii.InputStream `json:"body"`
    }

    iii.RegisterFunctionTyped(worker, "files::process", func(ctx context.Context, in upload) (map[string]any, error) {
    	bytes, err := io.Copy(io.Discard, in.Body) // an InputStream is an io.Reader
    	if err != nil {
    		return nil, err
    	}
    	return map[string]any{"filename": in.Filename, "bytes": bytes}, nil
    })
    ```

Finish each read before the handler returns. When the handler returns, the SDK cancels an
`InputStream` that the handler started to read and did not finish. See
[Manage the Stream lifecycle](#manage-the-stream-lifecycle).

## Return a stream

To return data as a stream, put the stream in the result. The caller receives an `InputStream` in
the same field. The handler's SDK sends the result first, and then writes the data into the pipe.

The SDK sends the same values as streams in a result and in a payload. For these values, see
[Send a stream in a call](../using-iii/streaming#send-a-stream-in-a-call).

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    async function* csvLines(reportId: string) {
      yield "id,total\n";
      for await (const row of db.rows(reportId)) yield `${row.id},${row.total}\n`;
    }

    worker.registerFunction("reports::export", async ({ report_id }: { report_id: string }) => ({
      report_id,
      csv: csvLines(report_id), // an async generator, a Readable, or a Web ReadableStream
    }));
    ```

  </Tab>

Keep the worker connected until the caller has read the stream. The worker that returns a stream
owns the pipe of that stream. See [Pipe ownership](../understanding-iii/streaming#pipe-ownership).

## Write to a received OutputStream

A caller can pass a sink, which is a destination of its own for the data. The handler receives the
sink as an `OutputStream` and writes the data to it. A sink receives bytes only, so write the data
with `write`. The caller's call resolves after the sink has received all the data.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    import type { OutputStream } from "iii-sdk";

    worker.registerFunction(
      "reports::render-pdf",
      async ({ report_id, out }: { report_id: string; out: OutputStream }) => {
        for await (const page of renderPages(report_id)) await out.write(page);
        // Returning closes `out`. Throwing aborts it, so the caller gets an error, not a short file.
      },
    );
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Python">
    ```python
    from iii import OutputStream

    async def render_pdf(payload: dict) -> None:
        out: OutputStream = payload["out"]
        async for page in render_pages(payload["report_id"]):
            await out.write(page)
        # Returning closes `out`. Raising aborts it, so the caller gets an error, not a short file.


    worker.register_function("reports::render-pdf", render_pdf)
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Rust">
    ```rust
    use futures::TryStreamExt;
    use iii_sdk::{Error, OutputStream, RegisterFunction};
    use schemars::JsonSchema;
    use serde::Deserialize;

    #[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
    struct RenderPdf {
        report_id: String,
        out: OutputStream,
    }

    worker.register_function(
        "reports::render-pdf",
        RegisterFunction::new_async(|req: RenderPdf| async move {
            let mut pages = render_pages(&req.report_id);
            while let Some(page) = pages.try_next().await? {
                req.out.write(&page).await?;
            }
            // Ok closes `out`. Err aborts it, so the caller gets an error, not a short file.
            Ok::<_, Error>(())
        }),
    );
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Go">
    ```go
    type renderPDF struct {
    	ReportID string            `json:"report_id"`
    	Out      *iii.OutputStream `json:"out"`
    }

    worker.RegisterFunction("reports::render-pdf", func(ctx context.Context, data json.RawMessage) (any, error) {
    	var req renderPDF
    	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &req); err != nil {
    		return nil, err
    	}
    	for _, page := range renderPages(req.ReportID) {
    		if err := req.Out.Write(ctx, page); err != nil {
    			return nil, err
    		}
    	}
    	// Returning closes Out. An error aborts it, so the caller gets an error, not a short file.
    	return nil, nil
    })
    ```

If the caller's sink fails, the handler's next `write` fails with `STREAM_CLOSED`. The sink can
receive no more data, so let the error stop the handler.

## Send messages

An `OutputStream` carries bytes and messages. `write` sends bytes. `send` serializes one value to
JSON and sends it as one message, in one text frame. Use a message for a value that is not part of
the byte data.

One stream can carry both. For example, a route that the HTTP worker calls sends the status and the
headers of its `response` as messages, and the body as bytes. For the two types of frames, see
[Bytes and messages](../understanding-iii/streaming#bytes-and-messages).

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    import type { OutputStream } from "iii-sdk";

    type Download = { path_params: { id: string }; response: OutputStream };

    worker.registerFunction("reports::download", async ({ path_params, response }: Download) => {
      // Messages: the HTTP worker reads the status and the headers from text frames
      await response.send({ type: "set_status", status_code: 200 });
      await response.send({ type: "set_headers", headers: { "content-type": "text/csv" } });
      // Bytes: the body
      for await (const line of csvLines(path_params.id)) await response.write(line);
      // Returning closes the response, which ends the body.
    });

    worker.observe(
      { function_id: "http::on-request", args: { method: "GET", path: "/reports/:id/csv" } },
      "reports::download",
    );
    ```

  </Tab>

    ```python
        await response.send({"type": "set_headers", "headers": {"content-type": "text/csv"}})
        # Bytes: the body

            await response.write(line)
        # Returning closes the response, which ends the body.


    worker.register_function("reports::download", download)
    ```

    ```rust
    use std::collections::HashMap;

    use iii_sdk::{Error, OutputStream, RegisterFunction, Source};
    use schemars::JsonSchema;
    use serde::Deserialize;
    use serde_json::json;

    #[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
    struct Download {
        path_params: HashMap<String, String>,
        response: OutputStream,
    }

    worker.register_function(
        "reports::download",

            req.response

                .await?;
            // Bytes: the body
            let csv = render_csv(&req.path_params["id"]).await?;
            req.response.write(csv.as_bytes()).await?;
            // Ok closes the response, which ends the body.
            Ok::<_, Error>(())
        }),
    ```

  <Tab title="Go">
    ```go
    type download struct {
    	PathParams map[string]string `json:"path_params"`
    	Response   *iii.OutputStream `json:"response"`
    }

    worker.RegisterFunction("reports::download", func(ctx context.Context, data json.RawMessage) (any, error) {
    	var req download
    	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &req); err != nil {
    		return nil, err
    	}
    	// Messages: the HTTP worker reads the status and the headers from text frames
    	if err := req.Response.Send(ctx, map[string]any{"type": "set_status", "status_code": 200}); err != nil {
    		return nil, err
    	}
    	headers := map[string]any{"type": "set_headers", "headers": map[string]string{"content-type": "text/csv"}}
    	if err := req.Response.Send(ctx, headers); err != nil {
    		return nil, err
    	}
    	// Bytes: the body
    	for _, line := range csvLines(req.PathParams["id"]) {
    		if err := req.Response.Write(ctx, []byte(line)); err != nil {
    			return nil, err
    		}
    	}
    	// Returning closes the response, which ends the body.
    	return nil, nil
    })

    worker.Observe(iii.Source{
    	FunctionID: "http::on-request",
    	Args:       iii.Args{"method": "GET", "path": "/reports/:id/csv"},
    }, "reports::download")
    ```

## Forward a stream

A handler can pass a stream that it received to another function. Put the stream in the payload of
the other call, and do not read it first. The SDK then sends the ref of the stream, so the data does
not go through the worker that forwards it.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    import type { HttpRequest } from "@iii-dev/helpers/http";

    worker.registerFunction("files::upload", async (req: HttpRequest) => {
      // request_body is an InputStream: pass it on without reading it
      const result = await worker.call({
        function_id: "files::process",
        payload: { filename: req.path_params.name, body: req.request_body },
      });
      return { status_code: 200, body: result };
    });

    worker.observe(
      { function_id: "http::on-request", args: { method: "PUT", path: "/files/:name" } },
      "files::upload",
    );
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Python">
    ```python
    async def upload(req: dict) -> dict:
        # request_body is an InputStream: pass it on without reading it
        result = await worker.call_async(
            {
                "function_id": "files::process",
                "payload": {"filename": req["path_params"]["name"], "body": req["request_body"]},
            }
        )
        return {"status_code": 200, "body": result}

    worker.register_function("files::upload", upload)
    worker.observe(
        {"function_id": "http::on-request", "args": {"method": "PUT", "path": "/files/:name"}},
        "files::upload",
    )
    ```

  </Tab>

    ```rust
    use std::collections::HashMap;

    use iii_sdk::{CallRequest, Error, InputStream, RegisterFunction, Source};
    use schemars::JsonSchema;
    use serde::Deserialize;
    use serde_json::json;

    #[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
    struct PutFile {
        path_params: HashMap<String, String>,
        request_body: InputStream,
    }

    let client = worker.clone();
    worker.register_function(
        "files::upload",
        RegisterFunction::new_async(move |req: PutFile| {
            let client = client.clone();
            async move {
                // request_body is an InputStream: pass it on without reading it
                let result = client
                    .call(CallRequest::new(
                        "files::process",
                        json!({ "filename": req.path_params["name"], "body": req.request_body }),
                    ))
                    .await?;
                Ok::<_, Error>(json!({ "status_code": 200, "body": result }))
            }
        }),
    );

    worker.observe(
        Source::function("http::on-request").args(json!({ "method": "PUT", "path": "/files/:name" })),
        "files::upload",
    );
    ```

    ```go
    	// RequestBody is an *iii.InputStream: pass it on without reading it
    	payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
    ```

An `OutputStream` that the handler has not used also travels as its ref. When the handler has
started to read the stream, or has built the stream itself, the SDK creates a new pipe, and the data
goes through the forwarding worker.

A forwarded pipe keeps its owner. See
[Pipe ownership](../understanding-iii/streaming#pipe-ownership).

## Abort a stream

Abort a stream when the handler cannot send all of its data. The reader then receives the data sent
before the abort, and then an error with the code `STREAM_ABORTED`. The error shows that the data is
incomplete.

A stream aborts in these cases:

- The handler calls `abort(reason)` on an `OutputStream`. If the socket of the stream is not open,
  `abort` opens it first, so the reader always gets the error.
- The handler throws after it used an `OutputStream` that it received. The SDK aborts the stream.
- A source that the handler gave to the SDK throws while the SDK reads it, for example a generator
  that fails. The SDK aborts the stream.
- The worker crashes or loses its connection. The engine aborts the stream.

The reader does not receive the `reason`. The engine sends its own text in place of it: see
[Close and abort](../understanding-iii/streaming#close-and-abort). Only a call that the SDK runs in
the same process keeps the reason. To tell the caller the cause, fail the call or put the cause in
the result.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    // Fail the stream, and still answer the call with the cause
    try {
      for await (const page of renderPages(report_id)) await out.write(page);
    } catch (err) {
      await out.abort(`render failed: ${String(err)}`);
      return { ok: false, error: String(err) };
    }
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Python">
    ```python
    # Fail the stream, and still answer the call with the cause
    try:
        async for page in render_pages(report_id):
            await out.write(page)
    except Exception as err:
        await out.abort(f"render failed: {err}")
        return {"ok": False, "error": str(err)}
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Rust">
    ```rust
    // Fail the stream, and still answer the call with the cause
    if let Err(err) = render_into(&req.out).await {
        req.out.abort(format!("render failed: {err}")).await?;
        return Ok(json!({ "ok": false, "error": err.to_string() }));
    }
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Go">
    ```go
    // Fail the stream, and still answer the call with the cause
    if err := renderInto(ctx, req.Out); err != nil {
    	_ = req.Out.Abort("render failed: " + err.Error())
    	return map[string]any{"ok": false, "error": err.Error()}, nil
    }
    ```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

For the errors that a reader gets, see
[Handle aborts and errors](../using-iii/streaming#handle-aborts-and-errors).

## Manage the Stream lifecycle

When the handler returns or throws, the SDK ends the streams that the handler received. The table
shows what the SDK does with each stream. Most handlers need no cleanup code.

| When the handler                    | An `OutputStream` that it received                                            | An `InputStream` that it received                          |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| returns, after it used the stream   | The SDK closes it.                                                            | The SDK cancels it if the handler did not finish the read. |
| throws, after it used the stream    | The SDK aborts it.                                                            | The SDK cancels it if the handler did not finish the read. |
| returns, and did not use the stream | The SDK closes it, so the caller's sink ends with no data.                    | The SDK does not change it.                                |
| throws, and did not use the stream  | The SDK does not change it.                                                   | The SDK does not change it.                                |
| put the stream in another call      | The SDK does not change it. The rules apply in the function that receives it. | The SDK does not change it.                                |

A handler uses an `OutputStream` when it writes to it, sends a message on it, or takes its native
API with `toWritable()` or `toWebStream()`. A handler uses an `InputStream` when it starts a read.

A cancelled `InputStream` cannot be read, and the engine closes the writer of the stream. A read
that still runs after the handler returns, for example in a task that the handler started, fails
with `STREAM_CLOSED`. An `InputStream` has no `keepOpen()`, so finish each read before the handler
returns.

The same rules apply when the SDK runs a call to a function of the same worker in the process,
without a pipe.

### Calls through an observer

One rule is different when a worker calls the handler through an observer. The SDK closes an
`OutputStream` that the handler did not use only when the handler returns no value (`null` or
`undefined`). When the handler returns a value, the SDK does not change the stream.

The worker that makes the call sets what it means when the handler returns a value and does not use
the stream. For example, the HTTP worker calls a route through an observer. When the route returns a
value and does not use `response`, the HTTP worker sends the value as a buffered response.

If the caller passed its own sink, a handler that returns a value must use or close the sink. If the
handler does not, the sink stays open, and the caller's call fails with `TIMEOUT` when its timeout
expires.

### Keep writing after the handler returns

A handler can return its result first and write to an `OutputStream` later. Call `keepOpen()` on the
stream before the handler returns. The SDK then does not close or abort the stream when the handler
returns or throws. Your code must close or abort the stream when the work ends.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    import type { OutputStream } from "iii-sdk";

    worker.registerFunction(
      "jobs::start",
      async ({ job_id, log }: { job_id: string; log: OutputStream }) => {
        log.keepOpen(); // this handler answers now and keeps writing
        void (async () => {
          try {
            for await (const line of runJob(job_id)) await log.write(`${line}\n`);
            await log.close();
          } catch (err) {
            await log.abort(String(err));
          }
        })();
        return { started: true };
      },
    );
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Python">
    ```python
    import asyncio

    from iii import OutputStream

    running: set[asyncio.Task] = set()


    async def start(payload: dict) -> dict:
        log: OutputStream = payload["log"]
        log.keep_open()  # this handler answers now and keeps writing

        async def write_log() -> None:
            async with log:  # closes on exit, aborts on an exception
                async for line in run_job(payload["job_id"]):
                    await log.write(f"{line}\n")

        task = asyncio.create_task(write_log())
        running.add(task)
        task.add_done_callback(running.discard)
        return {"started": True}


    worker.register_function("jobs::start", start)
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Rust">
    ```rust
    #[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
    struct StartJob {
        job_id: String,
        log: OutputStream,
    }

    worker.register_function(
        "jobs::start",
        RegisterFunction::new_async(|req: StartJob| async move {
            req.log.keep_open(); // this handler answers now and keeps writing
            tokio::spawn(async move {
                match run_job(&req.job_id, &req.log).await {
                    Ok(()) => req.log.close().await,
                    Err(err) => req.log.abort(err.to_string()).await,
                }
            });
            Ok::<_, Error>(json!({ "started": true }))
        }),
    );
    ```

  <Tab title="Go">
    ```go
    type startJob struct {
    	JobID string            `json:"job_id"`
    	Log   *iii.OutputStream `json:"log"`
    }

    iii.RegisterFunctionTyped(worker, "jobs::start", func(ctx context.Context, req startJob) (map[string]bool, error) {
    	req.Log.KeepOpen() // this handler answers now and keeps writing
    	go func() {
    		if err := runJob(ctx, req.JobID, req.Log); err != nil {
    			_ = req.Log.Abort(err.Error())
    			return
    		}
    		_ = req.Log.Close()
    	}()
    	return map[string]bool{"started": true}, nil
    })
    ```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

`keepOpen()` changes only what the SDK does with the stream when the handler returns. It does not
change when the caller's call resolves: when the caller passed a sink, the call resolves only after
the stream ends.

## Payload size

A call without a stream sends its payload in one JSON message and receives its result in another.
Each JSON message has a size limit. The limit applies to the envelope: the complete JSON message,
with the payload or the result inside it. The size is the number of bytes of the serialized UTF-8
JSON.

To send more data, use a stream. Only the ref of the stream counts toward the limit. See
[Send a stream in a call](../using-iii/streaming#send-a-stream-in-a-call).

### Limits

| Sender or receiver                | Limit                                     |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Rust, Node, Python, and Go SDKs   | **64 MiB**                                |
| Browser SDK                       | **16 MiB** to send, **16 MiB** to receive |
| Engine, per message from a worker | **64 MiB**                                |

A large message crosses the connection in WebSocket frames:

- The Rust, Node, Python, and Go SDKs send a message of **16 MiB** or less as one text frame. They
  send a larger message, up to and including 64 MiB, as one fragmented WebSocket text message.
- The browser SDK does not fragment messages, because the browser WebSocket API gives no control of
  frames.
- The engine sends each message larger than **1 MiB** to a worker as one fragmented text message
  with frames of 1 MiB, so that no frame is larger than the frame size limit of a worker.
- The engine accepts a message as one frame or as fragments.

Fragments do not change the function APIs.

### Receive limit of a worker

Before the engine sends a message to a worker, it compares the size of the message with the receive
limit of that worker. If the message is larger, the engine does not send it, and the caller gets the
error `payload_too_large`.

The engine sets the receive limit when the worker registers:

- A browser worker gets **16 MiB**.
- A worker that declares the `large-messages.v1` protocol feature gets **64 MiB**. The version that
  the worker reports has no effect. The Rust, Node, Python, and Go SDKs declare the feature. The
  browser SDK does not declare it.
- Each other worker gets **64 MiB** or **16 MiB**. The engine sets this limit from the SDK version
  that the worker reports. A worker that reports no version, or a version that the engine cannot
  read, gets **16 MiB**. Other features, such as `observe.v1`, do not change the limit.

### Messages over the limit

- The Rust, Node, Python, and Go SDKs do not send a message over **64 MiB**. The SDK refuses the
  message with the error `payload_too_large`, and the error message links to this section. The
  browser SDK does the same over **16 MiB**.
- The engine drops a message over **64 MiB** that a worker sends. The connection stays open, and the
  other calls on the connection continue. For a call, the worker that sent the call gets
  `payload_too_large` as the result. For a result, the caller that waits for the result gets
  `payload_too_large`. The engine cannot answer other messages, such as a call that expects no
  result, so it logs them.

The same limits apply to the events that the engine sends to the target of an observer. The engine
also keeps at most **64 MiB** of one observed event. This size includes each field that the
observers of the event capture, and `input` and `output` both count. The engine does not deliver an
event that is over a limit: the observer counts a `TOO_LARGE` drop, and the engine logs a warning.
See [Observers / Observed call size](../using-iii/observers#observed-call-size).

## Go and the browser SDK

The Go SDK and the browser SDK use the same stream model as the TypeScript SDK. Their APIs differ in
these points.

In Go:

- Each read method takes a `context.Context`. `Read` is the exception: it takes no context, so an
  `InputStream` is an `io.Reader`.
- `Lines`, `Messages`, and `Frames` return iterators. An early exit from the loop cancels the
  stream.
- After a read fails, each later read returns the same error.
- The package `github.com/iii-hq/iii/sdk/packages/go/iii/helpers/http` wraps the streams of an HTTP
  route. `iiihttp.Wrap(fn)` calls `fn` with a `StreamRequest`, which is an `io.Reader` over
  `request_body`, and a `StreamResponse` with `Status`, `Headers`, and `Write`. The SDK closes or
  aborts the response by the rules in [Manage the Stream lifecycle](#manage-the-stream-lifecycle).

In the browser:

- The API is the TypeScript API with Web streams only. A source is a `ReadableStream`, a `Blob`, a
  `File`, an async generator, or an `InputStream`. A sink is a `WritableStream` or an
  `OutputStream`. The only native API is `toWebStream()`.
- The ref helpers are in `iii-browser-sdk/protocol`.
- An abort closes the socket of the stream with code 4011, because a browser can send only code 1000
  or a code from 3000 to 4999. The engine treats 4011 as an abort. The `reason` that the reader gets
  is `channel writer aborted: closed with code 4011`.
- `write` resolves when the socket holds 1 MiB or less of unsent data. `close()` waits until the
  socket has sent all the data.
- Reads have no backpressure. A page cannot pause its socket, so the frames that arrive before the
  page reads them stay in memory. Read a stream as it arrives, or cancel it.
- The URL of a stream's socket keeps the query string of the engine URL, such as `?token=`.

Workers on different SDKs can send streams to each other. For workers on different SDK versions, see
[Mixed fleets](../upgrading/from-0-26-x#mixed-fleets).
